walkthroughs.body_html:
Further Mechanics — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Further Mechanics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Further Mechanics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A car travels 4 km north then 3 km east. What is its displacement magnitude?
options: 7 km
5 km
1 km
25 km

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
options: Acceleration
Momentum
Kinetic energy
Weight

mcqs.q: What happens to the current as it goes around a series circuit?
options: A current in the coil is what induces an emf in the magnet.
Current splits in half at the battery so each direction gets some.
Current gets used up by each component as it flows around the circuit.
It stays the same at every point — current is conserved.

mcqs.q: What is required to induce an emf in a coil using a magnet?
options: A changing magnetic flux linkage through the coil — the magnet (or coil) must be moving or the field must be changing.
Just having a magnet near the coil induces an emf, even when both are stationary.
Current splits in half at the battery so each direction gets some.
A current in the coil is what induces an emf in the magnet.

mcqs.q: Why does a metal spoon in hot water heat up faster than a wooden one?
options: Metal heats up faster because it has a lower specific heat capacity, requiring less energy per degree.
Metal heats up faster because it has more thermal energy to begin with.
Metals have higher thermal conductivity, so heat is transferred more rapidly through them.
A current in the coil is what induces an emf in the magnet.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Scalar”?
options: Rate of change of displacement with respect to time, measured in m s⁻¹.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Velocity”?

Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.

A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as velocity, force, or displacement.
